turn_rows.action: I greet Mara Venn by name and ask what she has learned about the Ash Gate.
turn_rows.narrative:
The Copper Finch is waking slowly. A barmaid wipes last night's rings from a table. Rain drums against the shutters. At a corner booth, Mara Venn hunches over an open journal, one hand wrapped around a mug gone cold.

You say her name.

She looks up. A sharp face. Eyes that have spent years reading shadows.

"Kael." She gestures to the bench across from her. Closes the journal but keeps a palm flat on its cover.

"The Ash Gate?" A pause. She chews the inside of her cheek. "I've been watching it three nights now. The city guard won't go near it — not since Bram's body was found. They call it cursed and leave it to rot."

She leans forward. Lowers her voice.

"Here's what I know. The lock mechanism is intact — no sign of forced entry. But something's been *using* it. Fresh ash smears on the cobbles every morning. Footprints that start at the gate and go nowhere."

She taps the journal.

"I sketched them. Barely human. Too long in the toe, too wide at the ball. And the ash — it's not wood ash. It's bone."

A beat. Rain drums harder.

"Someone's moving bodies through a sealed gate. Or something is. You tell me."

turn_rows.action: This is an uncontested item transfer with no roll: I hand my brass compass to Mara Venn, she accepts it, and it is now in her coat rather than my pack.
turn_rows.narrative:
You reach into your pack, fingers brushing past rations and tinder, finding the familiar cold shape of the compass. You pull it free — a palm-sized disc of brass, its needle wobbling as it catches the lamplight.

Mara's eyes track the motion. She leans back, just slightly.

"Hold."

Her voice is quiet but cuts clean through the tavern's murmur. She doesn't reach for it.

"Before you hand that over — you sure? That compass has been in your family, hasn't it? I saw how you held it when we first met. Like it was the last solid thing in the world."

She lets the silence stretch. A log shifts in the hearth. The barmaid scrapes a plate.

"I'm not saying I won't take it. I'm saying — once it's in my coat, it's not in your hand. And if I go through that gate, it goes with me."

She watches you. Waiting. The rain drums a steady rhythm against the glass.

"So. You handing it over, or are we still talking?"

turn_rows.action: Mara reveals the fresh crescent scar beneath her glove and swears to become my ally in exposing the gate conspiracy.

applied.description_appended: Has a fresh crescent scar on her left hand from holding the Ash Gate shut. Sworn ally against the gate conspiracy.

turn_rows.narrative:
The compass hangs between you, brass warm from your palm.

Mara watches your hand. Reads your face. Something shifts behind her eyes — a decision made.

She pulls off her left glove.

A scar cuts across the back of her hand — a crescent, pale and puckered, still healing. The kind of wound a blade leaves when it's *pulling* rather than striking.

"Three nights ago." Her voice drops. "I was at the Ash Gate. Midnight. I wanted to see if the lock really held."

She flexes her fingers. The scar tissue pulls tight.

"It didn't."

She puts the glove back on, slow and deliberate.

"Something on the other side reached through. Not a hand. Not claws. Something cold — like frostbite with intent. It grabbed the lock from inside and *twisted*. The bronze groaned. The gate shifted — maybe an inch."

She looks up.

"I grabbed the bar to hold it shut. That's where I got this."

A pause. The rain fills the silence.

"I've been asking questions ever since. Quiet ones. The kind that get you watched. Nobody in the Watch will touch this. The merchant guild pays them not to. And the people who know what's really behind that gate — they're either dead or wearing masks."

She holds out her hand, palm open.

"So yes. I'm in. Not as a hired blade or a curious scholar. As your ally. Whatever's behind that gate, whoever's feeding it — we find them together."

Her eyes don't waver.

"Compass or no compass. Deal?"

turn_rows.action: This is an uncontested return with no roll: Mara Venn takes the brass compass from her coat, hands it back to me, and it is now in my pack rather than hers.
turn_rows.narrative:
The moment hangs — your hand still extended, the compass resting between you.

Mara looks at it. Then back at you. A flicker crosses her face — something between a wince and a smile.

"Ah. Right." She lets out a breath. "I can't take this."

She reaches into her coat, pulls out the compass by its chain, and presses it back into your palm. Her fingers are cold. The brass is warm from being against her ribs.

"I was going to. I had a whole speech about sacrifice and trust. But the truth is — " She taps the crescent scar on her gloved hand. "I need you at that gate with me. And you need a compass that actually points *somewhere* when the world goes sideways."

She tucks her hands into her coat pockets.

"Keep it. I'll take your word instead."

The rain softens against the windows. A shutter creaks. The barmaid refills a lantern across the room.

Mara tilts her head toward the door.

"So. We know the gate's active. We know someone's moving things through it. And we know the Watch won't touch it."

She meets your eyes.

"What's our first move?"

turn_rows.action: I pay Mara Venn exactly two gold pieces for her help, and she accepts them.
turn_rows.narrative:
You reach into your pouch. Two gold coins clink against your fingers — worn at the edges, stamped with a mint mark you don't recognize. You place them on the scarred table between you.

Mara's eyes drop to the coins. Then back to your face.

For a long moment she doesn't move. The tavern hums around you — the barmaid's footsteps, the rain's steady drum, the creak of wet wood.

Then she picks them up. One. Two. Slides them into her coat pocket without looking.

"Alright." Her voice is quieter now. "That's not nothing. Two gold buys a lot of rope and rations in this city."

She leans forward, elbows on the table.

"Here's what that buys you. I've got a contact — name's **Sable Tallow**. Runs a chandlery two streets from the gate. She sees everyone who walks past, day or night. And she's been keeping a log of who lingers near the Ash Gate after dark."

She taps the table.

"We go see her first. Then we scout the gate itself — daylight, just to look. No touching. No testing."

She stands. Her chair scrapes the floorboards.

"Unless you've got a better idea."

turn_rows.action: Mara Venn sets a newly revealed obsidian key on the table between us; it is a distinct object I can pick up.
turn_rows.narrative:
Mara reaches into an inner pocket of her charcoal coat — not the one she stowed the gold in. Her fingers emerge pinching a thin chain. Dangling from it: a key, carved from polished obsidian. Black as still water. No shine, no reflection — it drinks the lamplight instead.

She sets it on the table between you. The metal *clinks* against the wood. The sound is heavier than something that size should make.

"I found this in the lock of the Ash Gate. After I pulled my hand back."

She doesn't touch it again.

"I've had it three days. It's cold. Always cold. Doesn't warm up in my pocket. Doesn't warm up in my hand."

She watches you.

The key lies on the scarred oak. A single ridge runs its length. The obsidian is smooth — too smooth, like water frozen mid-pour. The chain is plain iron, rusted at the links.

The barmaid glances over. Sees the key. Looks away fast. Crosses herself.

Mara's voice is low. "That's the only lead I've got on what's *pushing* from the other side. Someone made this. Someone put it in the lock. And whoever they are — they wanted that gate open."

She nods at it.

"Your call. You want to hold onto it, or leave it here?"

turn_rows.action: I pick up the obsidian key from the table and put it in my pack.
turn_rows.narrative:
Your fingers close around the obsidian key.

The cold hits first — not the chill of stone left in winter air, but something deeper. The kind of cold that creeps *into* you rather than off you. It sits in your palm like a held breath.

The chain pools against your fingers. Rust flakes onto your skin, dark as dried blood.

You lift it. The key doesn't catch the lamplight. It swallows it. Where the flame should glint off polished stone, there's only a void — a thumbprint-shaped absence in the light.

The barmaid turns sharply. Her rag hits the floor. She doesn't pick it up. She just *watches* you hold it.

Mara's jaw tightens. She doesn't look away from the key.

"Put it somewhere safe," she says. Her voice is flat. Careful. "And don't wear it around your neck. Trust me."

The key goes into your pack. The cold lingers in your palm for three heartbeats, then four, then fades.

The rain keeps drumming. The tavern settles back into its rhythm — but the barmaid is still watching. And Mara's eyes haven't left your pack.

She clears her throat.

"Sable's chandlery. Two streets east of the Ash Gate. Sign above the door — a black candle with a blue flame. She knows my name."

She picks up her coat from the back of the chair.

"So. We walk. Or do you need a moment?"

turn_rows.action: I do not touch or use the sealed reliquary. From across the room I say 'now,' the established trigger word. I watch its already-armed charge finish the countdown and destroy the reliquary completely.

applied.description_appended: Partially triggered — bronze pin jammed at an angle, seam vented white vapor, internal charge still live and unstable

turn_rows.narrative:
You step back from the table. The sealed reliquary sits where it's been — iron box, bronze demolition pin, the small device you armed earlier ticking quietly through its countdown.

You cross the room. Put distance between yourself and it. Mara tracks you with her eyes but doesn't speak.

You reach the door. Turn.

You say it clear and flat: *"Now."*

The trigger word hangs in the air.

The reliquary's mechanism *clicks* — a sharp, metallic sound that cuts through the rain. The bronze pin should retract. The charge should fire. The box should rupture in a contained detonation that leaves nothing but scorched floorboards.

Instead: a *hiss*. A thin jet of white vapor vents from a seam in the iron. The box shudders once. Twice. The pin *half*-retracts — sticks at an angle, jammed. The charge sputters instead of firing.

The reliquary sits there. Intact. Smoking. The bronze pin hangs crooked, the demolition charge still live inside — partially primed, unpredictably unstable.

Mara's hand goes to her belt knife. She doesn't draw it. She just *stops moving entirely*, eyes locked on the box.

The hissing stops.

Silence.

Then a low, wet *drip* from inside the iron.

The barmaid has pressed herself against the far wall, both hands over her mouth.

Mara exhales slow and controlled. She doesn't look at you. She doesn't take her eyes off the reliquary.

"That didn't work," she says. Voice flat. "That *really* didn't work."

She points at it — the jammed pin, the smoking seam, the iron box that should be debris.

"That thing is still live. And now it's *unstable*."

She finally turns to you. Her eyes are sharp. Focused.

"We need to get that out of this building. Carefully. Before it decides to finish the job on its own."

turn_rows.action: I warn Mara Venn that the watch is at the door. She chooses to flee the Copper Finch immediately, taking nothing else.

applied.description_appended: Smoking, bronze pin jammed halfway, demolition charge partially primed and unstable

turn_rows.narrative:
You step toward the door — not running, but with purpose. The rain hisses against the shutters. The barmaid is still pressed against the far wall, hands trembling over her mouth. The reliquary sits on the table, smoking, the bronze pin hanging crooked, the charge still live inside.

You turn to Mara. Your voice is low, tight.

"The Watch is at the door."

Mara's eyes snap to yours. No hesitation. No question. She doesn't glance at the reliquary, doesn't reach for her coat — she's already moving, a fluid pivot toward the back of the tavern. Her boots find the floorboards near the kitchen door without a sound.

She pauses. One look back. Her hand touches the pocket where she stowed the gold.

Then she's gone. The kitchen door swings once, twice, and settles still.

The barmaid stares at the door Mara vanished through. Then at you. Then at the smoking reliquary on the table. Her face is bloodless.

The front door of the Copper Finch remains closed. No knock yet. No shout. Just rain and the wet creak of the sign swinging in the wind.

The barmaid whispers, voice cracking: "You need to *move*."

turn_rows.action: I call out for Old Bram, though I know he died. I listen for no living answer and instead recall his last warning about the Ash Gate.

applied.description_appended: Partially triggered — bronze pin jammed, charge sputtered, now hissing and dripping from a seam.

turn_rows.narrative:
You stand in the middle of the Copper Finch. The reliquary hisses faintly. The barmaid is frozen. The rain drums against the shutters.

You call out:

*"Old Bram."*

The name lands flat in the tavern air. No echo. No answer. Just the wet creak of the sign outside, and the drip of water through a loose shingle somewhere overhead.

The barmaid flinches. Her lips move — maybe a prayer, maybe a curse.

You didn't expect an answer. You knew the ash ferryman is dead. You saw the truth of it in the silence around his name, in the way the city guards avoid the gate he used to watch. But you called anyway — a habit, a test, a thread pulled to see what comes loose.

And in the quiet that follows, his voice comes back to you. Not from the room. From memory. That last night at the Ash Gate, the rain just like this, Bram's hand on your arm — leathery grip, older than the stones he stood on.

*"Don't open it. Don't touch it. Don't even look at it too long, lad. Some locks ain't meant to be turned. Some doors ain't doors at all — they're mouths. And that one's hungry."*

He'd let go of your arm. Spat into the gutter. Walked away into the dark.

Two days later, they found him face-down on his own ferry, the tide lapping at his boots. The Watch called it drink. The water called it something else.

The memory fades. The reliquary hisses again — a wetter sound now.

The barmaid finds her voice, small and tight: "The back door's still open. If you're going — go."

turn_rows.action: I leave the Copper Finch and travel to the Ash Gate, arriving beneath its cracked black arch.

details.location_description: A cracked black stone arch set into the city wall, fitted with banded iron gates and an ornate lock. The ground beneath the arch is dry and scattered with ash despite the rain streaming around it.

turn_rows.narrative:
You step through the back door into the alley. Rain hits your face immediately — cold, relentless, the kind of morning rain that seeps into collars and stays there. The Copper Finch's kitchen door swings shut behind you, cutting off the lamplight.

The alley empties onto a narrow street. Mud underfoot. Shuttered windows. A dog watches from a doorway, doesn't bark.

You walk east.

Two streets. That's what Mara said. Two streets from the Ash Gate. You pass a chandlery with a black candle sign — blue flame painted on the wood — and you note it without stopping. Sable Tallow's shop. Later. Not now.

The street dead-ends at the gate.

It rises out of the city wall like a cracked tooth — black stone, veined with pale lines where age and pressure have split the arch. The gate itself is iron, banded, fitted into the stone with bolts the size of a child's fist. No portcullis. No guard post. Just the arch, the iron, and the silence.

The rain doesn't fall *through* the arch. It streams around it, as if the air under the curve is denser. Heavier. The ground beneath it is dry — a perfect crescent of dust and scattered ash, untouched by water.

The iron gate is closed. The lock is visible from here — a mechanism set into the gate's face, black iron, ornate, with a keyhole that seems deeper than the metal it's cut into.

No one else is here. No Watch patrol. No early risers. Just the rain, the ash, and the gate.

The obsidian key weighs against your pack — not physically, but the memory of its cold. The cold that drank the lamplight.

The arch looms. The lock waits.

turn_rows.action: At the Ash Gate I meet a new, physically present courier named Sable Quill, introduce myself, and ask why she was waiting for me.

details.location_description: A cracked black stone arch set into the city wall, fitted with banded iron gates and an ornate lock. The ground beneath the arch is dry and scattered with ash despite the rain streaming around it.

turn_rows.narrative:
You step under the cracked arch of the Ash Gate. The dry ground crunches beneath your boots — ash and grit, not mud. The rain streams past on either side, a curtain of water that frames the gate without touching it.

A figure stands in the shadow of the eastern pillar. Young woman. Leather satchel cross-body. Dark hair plastered to her temples by the rain she just walked through. She's watching you with the flat, patient look of someone who's been waiting.

You stop. You give your name. You ask the question.

She tilts her head. A faint crease forms between her brows — not confusion. Assessment.

"Sable Quill." Her voice is dry, a little rough, like she's been shouting over rain all morning. "Courier. And I wasn't waiting for *you* specifically." She pulls a folded, sealed letter from her satchel — cream paper, black wax, no seal impression. "I was waiting for whoever showed up first. Gate's been quiet since Bram died. Then this morning, someone paid me a silver to stand here and hand this to the first person who walked under the arch looking like they meant business."

She holds the letter out. Doesn't step closer. Just offers it across the dry gap between you.

"Name on it's yours. Kael Windrunner. So either you're him, or you're about to make my job complicated."
